title: “India Plans 100 New Ships to Cut $75 Billion Foreign Freight Bill:” Sarbananda Sonowal at ‘Sagar Samvad’ of National Shipping Board
subtitle:
Sarbananda Sonowal Launches NSB Website, Receives Annual Reports at Sagar Samvad
Mansukh Mandaviya, Shantanu Thakur Join Sonowal at the National Shipping Board’s Inaugural “SAGAR SAMVAD” in Delhi
Indian Flagged Ships 16-20% Costlier Than Foreign; NSB Panel Proposes Five-Pillar Fix at ‘Sagar Samvad’
body_text:
The National Shipping Board (NSB) held its first ‘Sagar Samvad’ on here today, using the day-long dialogue to press for a five-point roadmap including to add 100 vessels to India's foreign-dependent merchant fleet over the next five years, as expressed by the Union Minister of Ports, Shipping & Waterways (MoPSW), Sarbananda Sonowal during his speech.
The event, themed "Charting the Roadmap Towards Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047," was held at the Civil Services Officers Institute on Vinay Marg and drew senior officials, shipowners, financiers and young cadets from India's maritime training institutes. Sagar Samvad, which means "ocean dialogue," carries the board's motto as its theme line: "Wisdom in the Ocean, Progress in the Nation.”
The inaugural edition of Sagar Samvad was chaired by Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal, who launched the board's first official website. NSB Chairperson Sameer Kumar Khare used the session to submit the board's annual report for 2025-26, subcommittee reports containing the policy advice for the government to Sonowal, outlining the board's work since its reconstitution in May 2025.
"The National Shipping Board (NSB) is older than the ministry it advises , a statutory body constituted in 1958 with one job: make sure India's shipping policy is written only after listening to the people who sail it, own it and pay for it," Sarbananda Sonowal said. “Under the dynamic leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi , under the re-enacted Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, and the new National Shipping Board Rules, the mandate has been renewed and strengthened. That is exactly why a platform like ‘Sagar Samvad’ matters , bringing policymakers, industry captains, technocrats and civil society into one room to argue, test ideas and build intellectual consensus in the open as per the highest tradition of a thriving democracy like India. That consensus, and nothing else, is what will carry us to an Atmanirbhar Shipping Bharat by 2047.”
Also in attendance was Vijay Kumar, Secretary of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. Sonowal held a special interaction with trainee officers from maritime training institutes, taking questions from what organisers called the sector's "Yuva Shakti," or youth power. Sonowal also acknowledged the success of the Container Manufacturing Assistance Scheme, worth ₹10,000 crore, with global shipping major Maersk now ordering containers built on Indian soil.
"I welcome the National Shipping Board's five-point roadmap , fiscal reform, assured cargo support, access to competitive financing, regulatory streamlining and a genuine ease of doing business," Sarbananda Sonowal said. "Taken together, these are not five separate tasks ; they are the architecture of a nation choosing, at last, to own its own trade. Under the visionary leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, we are quadrupling our port capacity to 10,000 million tonnes a year by 2047. NSB's task is to ensure Indian shipowners stand inside that growth , not watching it sail past on someone else's deck.”
Later in the day, a session on "Maritime Labour Force : Opportunities and Challenges" was chaired by Union Minister of Labour & Employment and Youth Affairs & Sports, Mansukh Mandaviya . The session took up the state of India's seafaring workforce, among the largest in the world, against the board's own findings on wage taxation, pension gaps and welfare provisions facing Indian seafarers, tying the government's youth and labour policy directly to the country's maritime ambitions.
Speaking at the session, Union Minister Mansukh Mandaviya said, “India’s maritime sector has the potential to become a major engine of employment for our young workforce and position India as the world’s leading supplier of skilled seafarers. Under the leadership of our dynamic Prime Minister Narendra Mod i, we are expanding quality training capacity, with steps taken to strengthen industry-led skilling, create wider employment pathways, address gender disparity and equip our workforce with skills for emerging segments such as cruise shipping and advanced shipbuilding. A skilled and future-ready maritime workforce will be central to achieving our Maritime India Vision 2030 and building India’s shipbuilding capabilities under Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047.”
Union Minister Mansukh Mandaviya emphasised that India must leverage the expanding global demand for skilled maritime professionals to create high-quality employment opportunities for its growing youth population. He called for coordinated efforts among the government, maritime industry, trade bodies and training institutions to expand training capacity, strengthen market outreach for Indian seafarers and build future-ready skills. He also emphasised the need to address gender disparity in maritime employment, develop specialised talent for emerging segments such as cruise shipping and create a skilled workforce capable of supporting India's ambition to become one of the world's leading shipbuilding nations.
The Union Minister of State for Ports, Shipping and Waterways, Shantanu Thakur presided over a panel discussion titled "Augmentation of Indian Tonnage: Opportunities and Challenges.”
"India pays close to $75 billion every year in freight to foreign shipping lines, to move cargo as critical as our crude oil, our gas, our coal and our urea," Shantanu Thakur said. "That is not a performance problem for Indian shipowners , it is a competitiveness and demand-partnership problem. For India to become a Viksit Bharat by 2047, we cannot depend on the goodwill of others to secure our own trade routes. We must command our own waterline.”
The  session also featured addresses by Capt. M.P. Basin and C.V. Subbarao. The valedictory panel on tonnage augmentation saw Atul Jadhav, Vice-President of the Indian Maritime Foundation; Anil Devli, Chief Executive Officer of the Indian National Shipowners' Association and an NSB member; Capt. S.I.A.K. Azad, Nautical Adviser at the DGMA; Ashutosh Sharma, Chief General Manager at the International Financial Services Centres Authority in Gandhinagar; Rahul Modi, President of the Container Shipping Lines Association and an NSB member; and Capt. Pankaj Kumar, Managing Director of Diamond Blue Shipping Solutions.
Panelists said flying the Indian flag remains 16% to 20% costlier than operating under a foreign one, a gap they attributed to India's tax on ship imports and maintenance services, tax deducted at seafarers' wages, tax on freight and higher domestic capital costs , expenses foreign competitors do not carry. Yet under the sector's Right of First Refusal mechanism, Indian owners are still expected to match foreign freight rates to win cargo, the panel said.
The panel proposed a five-pillar roadmap: fiscal reform, assured cargo support, access to competitive financing, regulatory streamlining and improved ease of doing business (EODB). The measures, if adopted, could help India add 100 ships to its fleet within five years , a step toward the Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision, or MAKV, 2047 target of ranking among the world's top five ship owning nations, the panel argued.
In his welcome speech, NSB Chairperson, Sameer Kumar Khare said, “This entire effort draws inspiration from the vision of our Prime Minister, who has placed the Blue Economy at the centre of Viksit Bharat under the Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047. Under the decisive leadership of Shri Sarbananda Sonowal , that vision has translated into high-impact infrastructure, port modernisation, and green shipping reforms on the ground.”
The National Shipping Board (NSB) is a statutory advisory body under the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, that counsels the government on shipping policy, tonnage, seafarer welfare and port-linked maritime development.
The inaugural edition of ‘Sagar Samvad’ programme of NSB brought together maritime stakeholders, industry representatives and experts across three sessions, with discussions centred on the roadmap for Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047. One of the sessions focused on “Maritime Labour Force : Opportunities & Challenges”, covering employment generation, seafarer skills, workforce development and emerging opportunities in the sector. Another session, “Augmentation of Indian Tonnage : Opportunities & Challenges”, examined the need to expand India’s shipping fleet and strengthen the country’s maritime capacity. The deliberations provided a platform for industry and stakeholders to share perspectives on building a stronger, more competitive and future-ready Indian maritime sector.

ministry.name: Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways

enrichment.summary: At the inaugural 'Sagar Samvad' dialogue of the National Shipping Board (NSB) in Delhi, Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal announced a plan to add 100 ships to India's merchant fleet over five years to cut India's roughly $75 billion annual foreign freight bill. The NSB, a statutory body reconstituted under the re-enacted Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, submitted its 2025-26 annual report and proposed a five-pillar roadmap—fiscal reform, assured cargo support, competitive financing, regulatory streamlining and ease of doing business—to make Indian-flagged shipping competitive, since it is currently 16-20% costlier than foreign-flagged shipping. The event also launched the NSB's website and held sessions on maritime labour force development and tonnage augmentation, linking these to the Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 goals.
enrichment.context: India's dependence on foreign shipping lines to move nearly 90% of its trade by volume has long been a strategic and economic vulnerability, particularly for critical imports like crude oil, gas, coal and urea. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 replaced the colonial-era Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, and reconstituted the National Shipping Board—originally created in 1958—as a modernised statutory advisory body on shipping policy, tonnage and seafarer welfare. This release ties into the government's broader Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 (MAKV 2047), which aims to quadruple port capacity to 10,000 million tonnes annually and place India among the world's top five ship-owning nations. Related initiatives mentioned, such as the ₹10,000 crore Container Manufacturing Assistance Scheme, reflect a wider push for self-reliance (Atmanirbhar Bharat) in shipbuilding and logistics, reducing reliance on foreign freight and containers. The identified cost disadvantages for Indian-flagged vessels—taxes on ship imports, seafarer wage TDS, freight taxation and higher capital costs—highlight long-standing structural issues in India's shipping competitiveness that successive maritime policies have sought to address through fiscal and regulatory reform.

prelims_questions.question: The National Shipping Board (NSB), which advises the Government of India on shipping policy, is a statutory body constituted under which legislation?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states the NSB was originally constituted in 1958 under the Merchant Shipping Act and has now been reconstituted under the re-enacted Merchant Shipping Act, 2025.

prelims_questions.question: As highlighted at the 'Sagar Samvad' dialogue, approximately how much does India spend annually on freight paid to foreign shipping lines?
prelims_questions.explanation: Union Minister of State Shantanu Thakur stated that India pays close to $75 billion every year in freight to foreign shipping lines.

mains_questions.question: India remains heavily dependent on foreign shipping lines for its international trade despite being a major maritime nation. Discuss the structural factors responsible for this dependence and evaluate the measures needed to build a self-reliant Indian merchant fleet.

Examine the significance of the Maritime India Vision 2030 and Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision 2047 in strengthening India's port and shipping infrastructure. What institutional and fiscal reforms are necessary to achieve these targets?

study_notes.reason: The release combines a testable institutional and legal core (NSB's reconstitution under the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, MAKV 2047 targets, scheme figures) with substantial analytical material on India's shipping cost-competitiveness gap and the proposed five-pillar policy roadmap, making it genuinely dual-use rather than skewed to one side.

prelims.point: The National Shipping Board (NSB), originally constituted in 1958, has been reconstituted as a statutory advisory body under the re-enacted Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, advising on shipping policy, tonnage and seafarer welfare.
prelims.why_important: NSB predates its parent ministry and was recently reconstituted under new legislation - a distinctive fact suited to statement-based questions on statutory bodies.

prelims.point: The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 replaced the colonial-era Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, as India's primary shipping legislation.
prelims.why_important: Replacement of a long-standing colonial-era act with new legislation is a recurrent current-affairs-linked prelims theme (old law vs new law).

prelims.point: Maritime Amrit Kaal Vision (MAKV) 2047 targets placing India among the world's top five ship-owning nations and quadrupling port capacity to 10,000 million tonnes annually.
prelims.why_important: Specific numerical targets of MAKV 2047 could be tested in a statement-based or matching question on maritime vision documents.

prelims.point: The ₹10,000 crore Container Manufacturing Assistance Scheme supports domestic container manufacturing, with Maersk now ordering India-built containers.
prelims.why_important: Scheme name, outlay and a concrete beneficiary example make it a plausible objective-question item on self-reliance schemes.

mains.point: Indian-flagged vessels are 16-20% costlier to operate than foreign-flagged ones due to taxes on ship imports/maintenance, TDS on seafarer wages, freight taxation and higher domestic capital costs.
mains.analytical_use: Explains structural causes behind India's foreign-dependent merchant fleet; usable in questions on fiscal barriers to competitiveness or self-reliance in a specific sector.

mains.point: NSB's five-pillar roadmap - fiscal reform, assured cargo support, competitive financing, regulatory streamlining and ease of doing business - aims to add 100 ships to India's fleet within five years.
mains.analytical_use: Provides the 'way forward' component for questions on reducing India's freight import bill or achieving Atmanirbhar Bharat in shipping and logistics.

mains.point: India's near-total dependence on foreign shipping lines to move critical imports (crude oil, gas, coal, urea) represents a strategic vulnerability beyond the mere economic cost of the $75 billion annual freight outflow.
mains.analytical_use: Useful for linking shipping self-reliance to energy security and trade resilience arguments under Atmanirbhar Bharat.

both.concept: Right of First Refusal mechanism for Indian shipowners
both.prelims_angle: The definition and operation of the Right of First Refusal mechanism in allocating cargo to Indian-flagged vessels could be tested as a factual/conceptual item.
both.mains_angle: Highlights a policy contradiction: Indian owners are still expected to match foreign freight rates despite bearing structurally higher costs, useful for critically examining the gap between protectionist cargo-support policy and market reality.
